It is usually preferred over rifampin in the treatment of tuberculosis or other mycobacterial infections in AIDS patients, especially those treated with cytochrome P450 substrates including protease inhibitors or efavirenz.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Which pharmacological agent is recognized as a 'repository form' of the primary drug for leprosy, capable of maintaining inhibitory concentrations for several months?
options: Rifapentine
Suramin
Clofazimine
Acedapsone
Dapsone
correctOption: Acedapsone
optionExplanations: Rifapentine has a long half-life permitting once-weekly dosing in tuberculosis but is not classified as a 'repository' form providing months of coverage like acedapsone.
Suramin is used for trypanosomiasis and is not used in the treatment of leprosy.
Clofazimine is given orally and, while it does accumulate in tissues, it is not used as a repository injection for long-term prophylaxis.
Acedapsone is an injectable repository formulation of dapsone; it is slowly released from the injection site, maintaining effective therapeutic levels for months.
Dapsone is the standard oral agent and requires daily or monthly administration as part of MDT, rather than acting as a months-long repository itself.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: When managing a patient with leprosy who exhibits high-level resistance to Dapsone, what is the most common underlying molecular mechanism encountered?
options: The text does not specify dapsone resistance mechanisms; it only lists them for isoniazid and rifampin.
Mutations in the rpo gene
Mutations in the katG gene
Deletions in the inhA gene
Mutations in the pncA gene
correctOption: The text does not specify dapsone resistance mechanisms; it only lists them for isoniazid and rifampin.
optionExplanations: Per the reference material, specific molecular mechanisms (katG, inhA, rpo) are provided for INH and Rifampin, while the mechanism of dapsone resistance is not detailed beyond general terms.
Rpo gene mutations are associated with resistance to Rifampin, not dapsone.
KatG gene mutations are associated with high-level resistance to Isoniazid (INH), as this gene codes for the peroxidase needed to activate the drug.
InhA gene deletions are associated with low-level resistance to Isoniazid (INH), not dapsone.
PncA gene mutations are associated with resistance to Pyrazinamide, not dapsone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 390 (Book Page)-398: High-level resistance [to INH] is associated with mutations in the katG gene... Low-level resistance occurs via deletions in the inhA gene... [Rifampin] inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (encoded by the rpo gene).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Under the current WHO protocols for the management of leprosy, what is the primary clinical criterion used to classify an adult patient as Multibacillary (MB) for the purpose of initiating Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT)?
options: The presence of skin lesions showing central healing and well-defined borders.
The detection of more than five distinct skin lesions on physical examination.
The involvement of exactly two peripheral nerve trunks regardless of skin signs.
The presence of a single skin lesion with a positive lepromin test.
A history of previous treatment for paucibacillary leprosy within the last decade.
correctOption: The detection of more than five distinct skin lesions on physical examination.
optionExplanations: Lesions with well-defined borders and central healing are classically associated with tuberculoid (paucibacillary) leprosy, which involves fewer than five lesions and does not meet the MB criteria for the 12-month regimen.

The WHO simplifies classification for field use: Paucibacillary (PB) is defined as 1 to 5 skin lesions, while Multibacillary (MB) is defined as more than 5 skin lesions. This ensures that patients with a higher bacterial load receive the three-drug (Rifampicin, Dapsone, Clofazimine) 12-month regimen.
While nerve involvement is a component of leprosy diagnosis, the count of skin lesions (more than five) is the specific threshold set by the WHO to categorize a patient as MB for MDT purposes.

A single skin lesion is typically classified as paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, often managed with a shorter or less intensive regimen than MB leprosy. The lepromin test is a measure of cell-mediated immunity but is not the primary WHO criterion for MDT classification.
Previous treatment history does not define the current classification; the current clinical presentation (lesion count and smear positivity if available) dictates whether the patient is PB or MB.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): Drug regimens usually include combinations of dapsone with rifampin (or rifabutin, see prior discussion) with or without clofazimine. ... In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A patient undergoing the 12-month WHO-recommended regimen for multibacillary leprosy develops a distinct reddish-brown to nearly black skin pigmentation. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this expected pharmacological effect of the protocol?
options: A systemic drug-induced lupus erythematosus-like syndrome causing malar-like hyperpigmentation.
A type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the dapsone component of the therapy.
The accumulation of phenazine dye crystals within the reticuloendothelial system and skin.
The deposition of iron-containing heme breakdown products due to drug-induced hemolysis.
Excessive production of melanin stimulated by the enzyme-inducing effects of rifampin.
correctOption: The accumulation of phenazine dye crystals within the reticuloendothelial system and skin.
optionExplanations: While isoniazid (INH) is associated with a lupus-like syndrome, the standard leprosy MDT drugs (Rifampicin, Dapsone, Clofazimine) are not the typical triggers for this specific malar-type pigmentation.
Hypersensitivity to dapsone usually manifests as a rash or 'sulfone syndrome' (fever, malaise, jaundice), not as the characteristic red-black pigmentation associated with clofazimine.

Clofazimine is a highly lipophilic phenazine dye used in MB-MDT. It accumulates in macrophages and various tissues, including the skin and conjunctiva, leading to a dose-dependent, reversible skin discoloration that can range from pinkish-red to brownish-black.
Dapsone can cause hemolysis, leading to potential jaundice or pallor, but it does not cause the specific red-brown to black skin discoloration characteristic of the phenazine dye in the MB regimen.
Rifampin is a potent enzyme inducer, but it causes orange discoloration of body fluids (tears, sweat, urine), not the persistent red-black skin pigmentation described in leprosy protocols.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 393 (Book Page): Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA, causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: During the course of WHO Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for leprosy, a patient presents with sudden inflammation of pre-existing skin lesions and new-onset neuritis without systemic fever. In evaluating standard protocols, which management step is most appropriate for this specific complication?
options: Initiation of high-dose corticosteroids while continuing the prescribed MDT regimen.
Adding thalidomide to the regimen as it is the specific drug of choice for Type 1 reactions.
Switching the patient from the Multibacillary (MB) to the Paucibacillary (PB) protocol.
Increasing the monthly supervised dose of Rifampicin to twice a month to suppress the bacterial flare.
Immediate discontinuation of all MDT components to prevent further allergic reactions.
correctOption: Initiation of high-dose corticosteroids while continuing the prescribed MDT regimen.
optionExplanations: The clinical description indicates a Type 1 (Reversal) Reaction, characterized by inflammation of lesions and neuritis. Standard WHO protocol dictates the use of systemic corticosteroids (like prednisolone) to prevent permanent nerve damage, while the MDT must be continued.

Thalidomide is highly effective for Type 2 reactions (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum) but is not effective for Type 1 reactions. Furthermore, thalidomide is strictly regulated due to its teratogenic potential.
Classification (PB/MB) is determined at the start of therapy. A reaction does not change the classification but requires the addition of anti-inflammatory agents to the existing protocol.

Increasing the dose of Rifampicin is not part of the WHO protocol for reactions. Rifampicin has no significant acute anti-inflammatory effect and higher doses do not resolve the immunological Reversal Reaction.

Discontinuing MDT during a reaction is contraindicated as the reaction is an immunological response to the bacteria, not a drug allergy. Treatment must continue to ensure the eradication of the underlying infection.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 309 (Book Page): Corticosteroids can be considered anti-inflammatory drugs with an intermediate rate of action (ie, slower than NSAIDs but faster than other DMARDs). ... reserved for temporary control of severe exacerbations.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 28-year-old male with eight skin lesions and a positive skin smear for acid-fast bacilli is diagnosed with Multibacillary (MB) leprosy. Laboratory testing reveals he is severely deficient in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD). Which adjustment to the standard WHO MB-MDT protocol is required to avoid a life-threatening hematologic event?
options: Maintain the standard regimen but administer daily Vitamin B12 to protect the marrow.
Omit Dapsone from the regimen and utilize a combination of Rifampicin and Clofazimine.
Switch the patient to a 6-month PB regimen as G6PD patients cannot tolerate 12 months of therapy.
Double the daily dose of Clofazimine while omitting the monthly Rifampicin dose.
Increase the daily dose of Rifampicin while replacing Clofazimine with Chloroquine.
correctOption: Omit Dapsone from the regimen and utilize a combination of Rifampicin and Clofazimine.
optionExplanations: Vitamin B12 does not protect against oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; the only management is the avoidance of the offending oxidant drug (Dapsone).

Dapsone is a sulfone that causes oxidative stress. In G6PD-deficient patients, this results in significant hemolysis. The WHO protocol for such patients suggests omitting dapsone and continuing with Rifampicin and Clofazimine, often with the addition of alternative agents like Ofloxacin or Minocycline in some specialist guidelines.

The patient is clinically and bacteriologically Multibacillary (>5 lesions, smear positive). He must receive treatment for 12 months; shortening the duration to 6 months increases the risk of relapse and drug resistance.
Rifampicin is the most potent bactericidal drug in the regimen and should never be omitted if the patient can tolerate it. Monthly supervised Rifampicin is the cornerstone of MDT.

Chloroquine is an antimalarial and has no role as a substitute for clofazimine in leprosy MDT. Increasing the daily dose of Rifampicin does not compensate for the loss of the other two required drugs for MB disease and may increase toxicity.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): INH is hepatotoxic and may cause abnormal liver function tests, jaundice, and hepatitis. ... Hemolysis has occurred in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. [Context of Dapsone Page 392 (Book Page): Hemolysis may occur, especially in patients with G6PDH deficiency.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: In the WHO-recommended Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for leprosy, the Rifampicin component is administered as a single monthly supervised dose rather than a daily dose. What is the primary pharmacological and logistical rationale for this specific dosing protocol?
options: Intermittent dosing prevents the drug from inducing the hepatic CYP450 enzymes that would otherwise rapidly degrade Clofazimine.
To minimize the significant risk of light-chain proteinuria associated with daily Rifampicin ingestion.
Daily Rifampicin is strictly avoided to prevent the orange discoloration of urine, which causes poor patient adherence.
Its powerful bactericidal effect on M. leprae allows for effective intermittent dosing while ensuring patient compliance through supervision.
Rifampicin's half-life is significantly extended to over 30 days when used against M. leprae.
correctOption: Its powerful bactericidal effect on M. leprae allows for effective intermittent dosing while ensuring patient compliance through supervision.
optionExplanations: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer regardless of the interval, though induction is more pronounced with daily use. However, the schedule is designed for bacterial killing and resistance prevention rather than to protect Clofazimine metabolism.
While Rifampicin can cause light-chain proteinuria, this is a rare side effect and not the primary reason for the intermittent dosing schedule used in the leprosy protocol.
Orange discoloration of fluids is harmless. While patients are warned about it, the dosing schedule is determined by bactericidal efficacy and compliance management, not fluid color.

M. leprae is highly sensitive to Rifampicin. A single 600mg dose monthly kills the vast majority of viable bacilli. Logistically, this allows health workers to supervise the dose once a month, ensuring at least one effective drug is definitely taken, which prevents resistance to the daily dapsone.
Rifampicin has a relatively short half-life (about 3-5 hours). Its monthly use is based on its high bactericidal 'kill rate' against M. leprae, not on a long pharmacokinetic half-life.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone. ... Rifampin commonly causes light-chain proteinuria and may impair antibody responses.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: For an adult patient diagnosed with paucibacillary (PB) leprosy involving three skin lesions and no positive nerve smears, what is the standard WHO-recommended treatment regimen and total duration?
options: Daily Dapsone and Clofazimine for 12 months.
Monthly Rifampicin, daily Dapsone, and daily Clofazimine for 6 months.
Daily Rifampicin and daily Dapsone for 18 months.
A single dose of Rifampicin, Ofloxacin, and Minocycline (ROM).
Monthly Rifampicin and daily Dapsone for 6 months.
correctOption: Monthly Rifampicin and daily Dapsone for 6 months.
optionExplanations: This is a multibacillary regimen (due to Clofazimine) but the duration for MB leprosy is 12 months, and it would usually include Rifampicin. PB disease only requires 6 months.
The inclusion of Clofazimine defines the Multibacillary (MB) regimen. PB leprosy does not require Clofazimine, and the duration is 6 months, not 12.
18 months is excessive for PB leprosy and daily Rifampicin is not the WHO standard for this infection due to cost, supervision requirements, and the efficacy of monthly dosing for M. leprae samples.
Single-dose ROM was previously used for 'single-lesion PB leprosy' but current WHO recommendations favor the standard 6-month PB-MDT for all PB patients to simplify the program and ensure efficacy.
The WHO standard for PB leprosy (1-5 lesions) is a two-drug regimen consisting of Rifampicin (600mg once a month, supervised) and Dapsone (100mg daily, self-administered) for 6 months.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 395 (Book Page): Standard regimens— For empiric treatment of pulmonary TB ... [Context: Leprosy regimens Page 392 (Book Page): Drug regimens usually include combinations of dapsone with rifampin ... with or without clofazimine.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A patient on the multibacillary (MB) leprosy protocol experiences severe abdominal pain and clinical signs of small bowel obstruction. Crystal deposition in the lamina propria of the small intestine is suspected. Which component of the WHO MDT is responsible?
options: Clofazimine
Ofloxacin
Rifampicin
Dapsone
Ethambutol
correctOption: Clofazimine
optionExplanations: Clofazimine is highly lipophilic and can accumulate in the tissues as crystals. In high doses or prolonged MB therapy, it can deposit in the mesenteric lymph nodes and the lamina propria of the small intestine, leading to enteropathy and even intestinal obstruction.
Ofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone used only as a backup for leprosy; its GI side effects are typical of antibiotics (nausea/diarrhea) but do not involve bowel wall crystal deposition.
Rifampicin causes GI upset, but it is not known to form crystals in the bowel wall; its toxicity is primarily hepatic or immunological.
Dapsone toxicity primarily involves hematologic effects (hemolysis, methemoglobinemia) and skin reactions, not gastrointestinal crystal deposition or bowel obstruction.
Ethambutol is a first-line drug for tuberculosis, not a standard component of the WHO leprosy MDT. Its major toxicity is optic neuritis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 393 (Book Page): Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA, causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 45-year-old male who completed a 12-month course of Multibacillary (MB) MDT two years ago presents with several new anesthetic skin lesions and a worsening claw-hand deformity. Which finding would most strongly indicate a leprosy relapse requiring a new course of WHO MDT, rather than a late-onset Type 1 reaction?
options: The rapid appearance of lesions accompanied by significant edema and erythema.
The slow, insidious development of new non-inflamed lesions over several months.
A sudden decrease in the sensation of pre-existing lesions that were previously stable.
The presence of a low-grade fever and arthralgia suggesting a systemic flare.
A dramatic improvement in symptoms following a trial of high-dose prednisolone.
correctOption: The slow, insidious development of new non-inflamed lesions over several months.
optionExplanations: Rapid onset of inflamed, edematous lesions is the hallmark of a Type 1 (Reversal) Reaction, which is an immunological flare, not necessarily a sign of bacterial relapse.

M. leprae is extremely slow-growing. A relapse typically presents as the slow, insidious appearance of new, non-inflamed lesions long after therapy is completed. This suggests that dormant bacilli have begun to multiply again, requiring a new course of MDT.
Changes in pre-existing lesions during or after therapy are common in reactions as the body continues to clear bacterial antigens; new lesions are more indicative of relapse.
Systemic fever and arthralgia are more characteristic of Type 2 Reactions (ENL) rather than a simple bacterial relapse, which is often clinically 'quiet' except for new nerve/skin damage.
Improvement with corticosteroids confirms an inflammatory reaction (Type 1 or 2). A bacterial relapse would not resolve with steroids; indeed, steroids might worsen an active untreated infection.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 390 (Book Page): The chemotherapy of infections caused by Mycobacterium ... is complicated by ... the slow growth & intracellular location of mycobacteria; the chronic nature of mycobacterial disease.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: The metabolic activation and elimination of dapsone, a required daily component of the WHO leprosy protocol, involves hepatic N-acetylation. How does the genetic polymorphism of N-acetyltransferase affect the implementation of the standard WHO protocol?
options: Slow acetylators must be given twice the monthly Rifampicin dose to compensate for poor dapsone activity.
While half-life varies between fast and slow acetylators, the standard WHO doses are generally fixed, though slow acetylators have a higher risk of methemoglobinemia.
Fast acetylators require the addition of a second monthly supervised Rifampicin dose to the 12-month MB regimen.
Slow acetylators must be switched to an 18-month PB regimen to avoid lethal sulfone syndrome.
Fast acetylators are the only group that can be treated with the 6-month PB protocol, as slow acetylators require 12 months.
correctOption: While half-life varies between fast and slow acetylators, the standard WHO doses are generally fixed, though slow acetylators have a higher risk of methemoglobinemia.
optionExplanations: Rifampicin dosing is not adjusted based on dapsone acetylation status. The monthly 600mg Rifampicin dose is a fixed standard to ensure bactericidal kill regardless of dapsone kinetics.

Dapsone (like Isoniazid) is acetylated. Slow acetylators maintain higher blood levels for longer, which increases the risk of dose-dependent toxicities like methemoglobinemia and hemolysis, but the WHO protocol maintains a standard 100mg dose for operational feasibility.
A second monthly dose is not part of the standard WHO protocol for fast acetylators; the program is designed for simplicity in field conditions using fixed-dose blister packs.
Acetylation status does not dictate the PB/MB classification or the duration of therapy, which are based on lesion count and bacterial load.
PB vs MB status is clinical. Acetylation status might influence side effect monitoring but does not change the 6-month PB or 12-month MB treatment duration protocol.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 390 (Book Page): The liver metabolism of INH is by acetylation and is under genetic control. Patients may be fast or slow inactivators of the drug. ... [Context: Dapsone Page 392 (Book Page): undergoes enterohepatic cycling, and is eliminated in the urine, partly as acetylated metabolites.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: What is the primary biochemical target of Dapsone within the folate synthesis pathway of Mycobacterium leprae as utilized in the WHO MDT protocol?
options: Dihydropteroate synthase
Dihydrofolate reductase
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Thymidylate synthase
Arabinosyltransferase
correctOption: Dihydropteroate synthase
optionExplanations: Dapsone is a sulfone that acts as a structural analog of PABA, competitively inhibiting the enzyme dihydropteroate synthase in the folic acid synthesis pathway of M. leprae.
Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by trimethoprim and pyrimethamine, not by dapsone or other sulfones/sulfonamides.
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is inhibited by Rifampicin, the other primary component of the leprosy MDT.
Thymidylate synthase is the target of 5-fluorouracil (a pyrimidine antimetabolite), not dapsone.
Arabinosyltransferase is inhibited by Ethambutol, which is used for tuberculosis but not in the standard WHO leprosy protocols.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): Dapsone ... The mechanism of action of sulfones may involve inhibition of folic acid synthesis.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
coreConcept: WHO Standard Multidrug Therapy (MDT) for Leprosy
statement: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended protocols for the management of multibacillary leprosy, which combination of drugs constitutes the standard multidrug therapy (MDT)?
options: Dapsone, Rifabutin, and Streptomycin
Dapsone and Rifampin
Rifampin, Clofazimine, and Pyrazinamide
Dapsone, Rifampin, and Clofazimine
Dapsone, Clofazimine, and Ethambutol
correctOption: Dapsone, Rifampin, and Clofazimine
optionExplanations: Streptomycin is used for severe tuberculosis or drug-resistant strains but is not a component of the standard WHO leprosy protocol.
The dual combination of Dapsone and Rifampin is the standard WHO protocol for paucibacillary leprosy, not multibacillary leprosy.
Pyrazinamide is used for short-course tuberculosis treatment and is not part of the standard MDT for leprosy.
WHO recommends a triple-drug regimen of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for multibacillary leprosy to prevent the emergence of drug resistance and ensure the eradication of M. leprae.
Ethambutol is a first-line drug for tuberculosis, not a standard component of the WHO MDT for leprosy.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 393 (Book Page): [Drug regimens usually include combinations of dapsone with rifampin (or rifabutin, see prior discussion) with or without clofazimine.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Dapsone is characterized as the most active agent against Mycobacterium leprae. Which biochemical mechanism best explains its primary bacteriostatic effect?
options: Inhibition of the synthesis of mycolic acids
Formation of quinoline-quinone metabolites acting as cellular oxidants
Blockade of the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis
Inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase in folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
correctOption: Inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase in folic acid synthesis
optionExplanations: Inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis is the primary mechanism of isoniazid, which is used for tuberculosis.
Formation of reactive oxidants is the mechanism associated with primaquine, used in malaria treatment, rather than the folic acid antagonism of dapsone.
The 30S ribosomal subunit is targeted by aminoglycosides like streptomycin, not by dapsone.

Dapsone is a sulfone that acts similarly to sulfonamides by competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase, thereby blocking the synthesis of folic acid essential for bacterial nucleic acid production.
Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is the mechanism of action for rifampin, not dapsone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): [Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae. The mechanism of action of sulfones may involve inhibition of folic acid synthesis.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
coreConcept: WHO Leprosy Protocol Contrast (PB vs MB)
statement: In comparing the WHO management protocols for paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy, what is the most significant pharmacological distinction regarding the inclusion of clofazimine?
options: Clofazimine is excluded in multibacillary leprosy due to skin discoloration
Clofazimine is only used topically in paucibacillary disease
Clofazimine is used to prevent the neuropathy associated with dapsone
Clofazimine is added to the multibacillary regimen to enhance mycobacterial DNA interaction
Clofazimine is substituted for rifampin in paucibacillary cases
correctOption: Clofazimine is added to the multibacillary regimen to enhance mycobacterial DNA interaction
optionExplanations: Clofazimine does cause skin discoloration, but this is a side effect, not the reason for its exclusion; it is actually a requirement in multibacillary regimens.
Clofazimine is administered orally, not topically, and is generally reserved for multibacillary or resistant cases.
Clofazimine does not prevent dapsone-induced neuropathy; rather, dapsone-induced neuropathy is managed by pyridoxine if it resembles isoniazid toxicity.

The WHO adds clofazimine, a phenazine dye that interacts with bacterial DNA, specifically to the triple-drug regimen for multibacillary leprosy to manage the higher bacterial load and prevent resistance.
Rifampin is never substituted by clofazimine; rifampin is the cornerstone of both paucibacillary and multibacillary protocols.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 393 (Book Page): [Drug regimens usually include combinations of dapsone with rifampin... with or without clofazimine. Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA...]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 29-year-old male from a rural endemic region presents with several anesthetic skin lesions and thickened peripheral nerves. He is started on the WHO multidrug therapy for leprosy. Within 48 hours, he develops severe fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine. Laboratory findings reveal a significant drop in hemoglobin and the presence of Heinz bodies. Which drug-host interaction is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
options: Dapsone-induced hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Acedapsone-induced methemoglobinemia
Clofazimine-induced intestinal malabsorption
Rifampin-induced hepatic enzyme induction
Rifampin-induced light-chain proteinuria
correctOption: Dapsone-induced hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
optionExplanations: Dapsone is a known oxidizing agent. In patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, dapsone causes oxidative stress on red blood cells, leading to hemolysis, jaundice, and Heinz body formation.
While acedapsone can cause methemoglobinemia, the combination of jaundice and Heinz bodies specifically points to acute hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient individual.
Clofazimine primarily causes skin discoloration and GI irritation, not an acute hemolytic crisis.
Rifampin can cause liver dysfunction, but it does not typically cause acute hemolysis with Heinz bodies.
Rifampin can cause light-chain proteinuria, but this is a renal/immunologic finding, not a cause of jaundice or hemolytic anemia.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): [Dapsone... Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal irritation, fever, skin rashes, and methemoglobinemia. Hemolysis may occur, especially in patients with G6PDH deficiency.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: The inclusion of clofazimine in the WHO multibacillary leprosy regimen is often associated with a distinct dermatological change. Which of the following best describes this pharmacological effect?
options: Permanent orange staining of contact lenses
Dose-dependent photosensitivity and thinning of the skin
Immediate urticarial rash requiring drug cessation
Red-brown to black skin discoloration
Acneiform eruptions similar to those seen with isoniazid
correctOption: Red-brown to black skin discoloration
optionExplanations: Orange staining of tears and contact lenses is a characteristic effect of rifampin, not clofazimine.
Photosensitivity is more common with tetracyclines or pyrazinamide, while clofazimine is noted specifically for its pigmentary changes.
Urticaria can occur with many drugs but is not the characteristic dermatological effect of clofazimine.
Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that accumulates in the skin and tissues, causing a dose-dependent discoloration that ranges from red-brown to nearly black.
Dapsone, not clofazimine, is used at low doses to treat acne, and isoniazid is not the primary cause of such eruptions among antimycobacterials.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 393 (Book Page): [Clofazimine... causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: What is the clinical significance of acedapsone in the long-term management of leprosy infections?
options: It is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor used for multidrug resistance
It is a topical form used specifically for anesthetic skin lesions
It is an alternative to rifampin in HIV-leprosy coinfections
It is an oral prodrug that prevents dapsone resistance
It is a repository form providing inhibitory levels for several months
correctOption: It is a repository form providing inhibitory levels for several months
optionExplanations: Acedapsone, like dapsone, is a dihydropteroate synthase inhibitor, not a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (like pyrimethamine).
Acedapsone is administered parenterally, not topically, and acts systemically against the infection.
Rifabutin, not acedapsone, is the preferred alternative for rifampin in the context of certain coinfections involving cytochrome P450 substrates.
Acedapsone is a repository form, not an oral prodrug designed specifically to prevent resistance.
Acedapsone is the repository injectable form of dapsone, which releases the active drug slowly, maintaining inhibitory concentrations in the blood for several months, aiding in compliance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): [Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: In the standard WHO multidrug therapy for leprosy, rifampin is often administered once monthly rather than daily. What is the primary clinical rationale for this intermittent dosing in the leprosy protocol?
options: To maximize its renal clearance and prevent nephrotoxicity
To decrease the risk of a flu-like syndrome and delay resistance
To exploit its high oral bioavailability which exceeds 99%
To ensure it does not induce hepatic enzymes for dapsone metabolism
To avoid permanent orange staining of the skin and urine
correctOption: To decrease the risk of a flu-like syndrome and delay resistance
optionExplanations: Rifampin is primarily eliminated via biliary excretion and hepatic metabolism, not renal clearance.

In leprosy management, rifampin is given monthly in supervised doses to delay the emergence of resistance to dapsone while minimizing toxicity such as the flu-like syndrome associated with frequent intermittent dosing.
While rifampin has good bioavailability, the dosing frequency is determined by resistance patterns and the organism's slow growth rate, not solely its absorption percentage.
Rifampin induces hepatic enzymes even with intermittent dosing; it cannot be 'avoided' by monthly administration.
Rifampin colors sweat, urine, and tears orange regardless of the frequency of dosing; this is a harmless side effect.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): [In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 40-year-old patient with AIDS is being treated with a protease inhibitor-based HAART regimen and is recently diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy. According to pharmacological principles, which modification to the standard WHO leprosy protocol is most appropriate to avoid major drug-drug interactions?
options: Administer streptomycin as a repository intramuscular injection
Use rifabutin instead of rifampin to minimize P450 induction
Increase the dose of dapsone to 500mg daily
Substitute dapsone with clofazimine monotherapy
Omit clofazimine to prevent potentiation of the protease inhibitor
correctOption: Use rifabutin instead of rifampin to minimize P450 induction
optionExplanations: Streptomycin does not address the multibacillary requirement for a rifamycin-class drug and does not solve the P450 induction problem.

Rifampin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450, which would drastically reduce the levels of protease inhibitors. Rifabutin is preferred because it is a less potent enzyme inducer and more compatible with HAART.
Increasing the dapsone dose would increase toxicity (methemoglobinemia and hemolysis) without addressing the underlying enzyme induction issue caused by rifamycins.
Monotherapy is contraindicated in leprosy due to the high risk of developing drug resistance.
Clofazimine does not significantly interact with protease inhibitors; it is the rifamycin component (rifampin) that necessitates the modification.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): [Rifabutin is equally effective as an antimycobacterial agent and is less likely to cause drug interactions than rifampin. It is usually preferred over rifampin... in AIDS patients, especially those treated with cytochrome P450 substrates including protease inhibitors...]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: The pharmacological management of leprosy involves the liver metabolism of dapsone. Which physiological/metabolic loop is shared between dapsone and isoniazid (INH)?
options: Reductive bioactivation by bacterial ferredoxins
Metabolism by xanthine oxidase into uric acid
Glucuronidation followed by biliary excretion
Hydrolysis by plasma cholinesterases
Acetylation in the liver, influenced by genetic polymorphisms
correctOption: Acetylation in the liver, influenced by genetic polymorphisms
optionExplanations: Reductive bioactivation by ferredoxins is the mechanism for metronidazole and tinidazole, not dapsone.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in the metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine and allopurinol, not dapsone or INH.
Glucuronidation is the primary pathway for drugs like morphine, but not the defining shared pathway for INH and dapsone.
Plasma cholinesterase is involved in the metabolism of succinylcholine and mivacurium, not antimycobacterials.
Both isoniazid (INH) and dapsone are metabolized in the liver via N-acetylation. This pathway is subject to genetic polymorphism, resulting in 'fast' and 'slow' acetylator phenotypes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page): [The liver metabolism of INH is by acetylation and is under genetic control... [Dapsone] is eliminated in the urine, partly as acetylated metabolites.]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Which of the following is an accurate biochemical fact regarding Clofazimine, as used in the treatment of leprosy?
options: It is a prodrug requiring bioactivation by pyrazinamidases
It is a synthetic 4-aminoquinoline that inhibits heme polymerization
It acts as a suicide substrate for ATP synthase
It is a phenazine dye that likely interacts with mycobacterial DNA
It inhibits arabinosyltransferase involved in cell wall synthesis
correctOption: It is a phenazine dye that likely interacts with mycobacterial DNA
optionExplanations: Pyrazinamide requires bioactivation by pyrazinamidases, not clofazimine.
4-aminoquinoline describes chloroquine, used in malaria and some amebiasis cases, but not clofazimine.
Bedaquiline inhibits ATP synthase, not clofazimine.
Clofazimine is biochemically a phenazine dye. Its mechanism of action, though not fully elucidated, is believed to involve binding to and interacting with the DNA of Mycobacterium leprae.
Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyltransferase; clofazimine's target is thought to be DNA-related.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 392 (Book Page)-400: [Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA...]

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Which combination of agents is currently recommended by the WHO as the standard multi-drug therapy (MDT) for the management of multibacillary leprosy to prevent the emergence of resistance?
options: Dapsone and Ethambutol
Streptomycin and Pyrazinamide
Clofazimine and Bithionol
Rifampin and Isoniazid
Rifampin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine
correctOption: Rifampin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine
optionExplanations: While Dapsone is used in leprosy, Ethambutol is a first-line antitubercular agent and is not part of the standard leprosy MDT.
Streptomycin and Pyrazinamide are primary drugs for Tuberculosis; Streptomycin is only an alternative for severe Mycobacterium tuberculosis cases.
Clofazimine is used in leprosy, but Bithionol is an antihelminthic drug used for Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke).
Rifampin and Isoniazid are the core drugs for the treatment of Tuberculosis, not the standard WHO protocol for leprosy.
Correct. Standard WHO protocol for multibacillary leprosy involves a combination of Rifampin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine to enhance efficacy and prevent resistance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Because of increasing reports of resistance, it is recommended that the drug [dapsone] be used in combinations with rifampin and/or clofazimine (see below).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which Dapsone exerts its bactericidal effect against Mycobacterium leprae?
options: Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase via rpo gene binding
Inhibition of ATP synthase within the mycobacterial mitochondria
Inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase resulting in folic acid synthesis blockade
Blockade of arabinosyltransferases involved in cell wall synthesis
Direct interaction with DNA resulting in cross-linking of strands
correctOption: Inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase resulting in folic acid synthesis blockade
optionExplanations: Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is the mechanism of action for Rifampin, not Dapsone.
Bedaquiline inhibits ATP synthase; this mechanism is not associated with standard leprosy drugs like Dapsone.
Correct. Dapsone is a sulfone that acts as an antimetabolite of PABA, inhibiting the enzyme dihydropteroate synthase in the folic acid synthesis pathway.
Inhibition of arabinosyltransferases is the mechanism of Ethambutol, a first-line drug for Tuberculosis.
Direct DNA interaction and cross-linking is the mechanism associated with alkylating agents or Clofazimine (partially), not the primary effect of Dapsone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae. The mechanism of action of sulfones may involve inhibition of folic acid synthesis.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A patient being treated for leprosy presents with a striking red-brown to nearly black discoloration of the skin. Which drug in the standard MDT protocol is responsible for this effect?
options: Acedapsone
Rifampin
Ethionamide
Clofazimine
Dapsone
correctOption: Clofazimine
optionExplanations: Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone; it shares the toxicity profile of dapsone and does not cause deep skin pigmentation.
Rifampin is known to color sweat, urine, and tears orange, but it does not cause generalized dark skin discoloration.
Ethionamide is a second-line drug for tuberculosis; its primary adverse effects are gastrointestinal irritation and neurologic effects.
Correct. Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that accumulates in tissues, leading to a distinctive skin discoloration that can range from red-brown to black.
Dapsone commonly causes skin rashes and methemoglobinemia, but not the characteristic red-brown/black pigmentation of Clofazimine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 400 (Book Page): Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA, causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 42-year-old male from a rural endemic area presents with six symmetrical, erythematous, anesthetic skin nodules on his extremities and trunk. Slit-skin smears are positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB index 3+). His vitals are BP 115/75 mmHg and HR 78 bpm. According to the WHO recommendations for managing this specific classification of leprosy, which protocol is most appropriate?
options: Dapsone monotherapy for a minimum of 24 months
Rifampin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine for 12 months
Single dose of Rifampin, Ofloxacin, and Minocycline
Rifampin and Dapsone for 6 months
Streptomycin, Isoniazid, and Rifampin for 18 months
correctOption: Rifampin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine for 12 months
optionExplanations: Monotherapy for leprosy is strictly contraindicated in the modern era due to the rapid emergence of resistance.
Correct. Patients with more than five lesions or positive skin smears are classified as multibacillary and require the three-drug regimen (Rifampin, Dapsone, Clofazimine) for 12 months.
ROM (Rifampin, Ofloxacin, Minocycline) was used for single-lesion paucibacillary leprosy, not for a patient with 6 lesions and a positive AFB index.
Rifampin and Dapsone for 6 months is the protocol for Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy; this patient has >5 lesions and is AFB-positive, classifying him as Multibacillary (MB).
This is a tuberculosis regimen and is not appropriate for the treatment of Mycobacterium leprae.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Because of increasing reports of resistance, it is recommended that the drug [dapsone] be used in combinations with rifampin and/or clofazimine (see below).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: In the management of leprosy, what is the primary clinical rationale for administering Rifampin as a monthly pulse dose rather than as a daily medication?
options: To reduce the risk of orange discoloration of the skin and urine
To maximize its effect on DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and delay Dapsone resistance
To minimize the risk of G6PD-mediated hemolytic anemia
To prevent the induction of hepatic P450 enzymes that would clear Dapsone
To increase the oral bioavailability of concomitant Clofazimine
correctOption: To maximize its effect on DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and delay Dapsone resistance
optionExplanations: Discoloration of fluids is a benign side effect of Rifampin; the dosing schedule is designed for therapeutic efficacy and resistance prevention, not cosmetic reasons.
Correct. Rifampin is a potent bactericidal agent; in leprosy protocols, monthly administration is sufficient to significantly delay the development of resistance to Dapsone.
Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency is a characteristic toxicity of Dapsone, not Rifampin.
While Rifampin induces P450 enzymes, the monthly dosing in leprosy is specifically utilized to manage resistance rather than to prevent induction.
Rifampin dosing does not significantly impact the bioavailability of Clofazimine, which is a separate component of the MDT.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Which specific pharmacological formulation provides inhibitory plasma concentrations of dapsone for several months following a single intramuscular injection in the treatment of leprosy?
options: Clofazimine
Dapsone Furoate
Diaminodiphenylsulfone
Acedapsone
Rifapentine
correctOption: Acedapsone
optionExplanations: Clofazimine is a separate phenazine dye drug used in MDT, not a repository form of dapsone.
Diloxanide furoate is a luminal amebicide; no 'Dapsone Furoate' exists as a standard repository formulation.
Diaminodiphenylsulfone is the chemical name for standard dapsone, which has a much shorter half-life and requires daily oral dosing.
Correct. Acedapsone is the repository (depot) form of dapsone, designed to provide long-lasting inhibitory concentrations from a single dose.
Rifapentine is a rifamycin used for tuberculosis that allows for once-weekly dosing, but it is not a repository form of dapsone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A leprosy patient develops Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), a severe immunologic reaction characterized by fever and painful skin nodules. Which agent is indicated for the management of this specific complication?
options: Suramin
Metronidazole
Sodium Stibogluconate
Albendazole
Thalidomide
correctOption: Thalidomide
optionExplanations: Suramin is used for the early stages of African trypanosomiasis and is not used for ENL.
Metronidazole is an antiprotozoal and anaerobic antibacterial agent with no role in leprosy reactions.
Sodium stibogluconate is used for leishmaniasis, not for the immunologic reactions associated with leprosy.
Albendazole is an antihelminthic drug used for nematodes and tapeworms.
Correct. Thalidomide is effectively used to treat ENL due to its complex immune-modulating effects, including the suppression of TNF-alpha.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 460 (Book Page): Thalidomide is used for some forms of leprosy, for immunologic diseases (eg, systemic lupus), and as an anticancer drug.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 31-year-old male patient on therapy for leprosy presents with headache, nausea, and cyanosis. Blood drawn for analysis appears chocolate-brown. Laboratory results show a methemoglobin level of 25%. Which component of the WHO leprosy protocol is most likely responsible for this biochemical finding?
options: Dapsone
Rifampin
Minocycline
Ethionamide
Clofazimine
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Correct. Dapsone is a well-known oxidant drug that can cause methemoglobinemia, especially at higher doses, leading to 'chocolate-colored' blood and cyanosis.
Rifampin is associated with orange fluid discoloration and hepatotoxicity, not methemoglobinemia.
Minocycline is a tetracycline that may be used as an alternative in leprosy but is not a common cause of methemoglobinemia.
Ethionamide is used for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and typically causes GI irritation and neurologic adverse effects.
Clofazimine causes skin discoloration and GI distress, but it is not typically associated with methemoglobinemia.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Common adverse effects [of dapsone] include gastrointestinal irritation, fever, skin rashes, and methemoglobinemia.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: What is the biochemical basis for the effectiveness of Clofazimine in the multidrug therapy of leprosy?
options: Interaction with DNA and possible inhibition of template function
Inhibition of the M2 proton channel to prevent viral uncoating
Blockade of the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis
Alteration of the cell membrane permeability via ergosterol binding
Inhibition of folic acid synthesis by competing with PABA
correctOption: Interaction with DNA and possible inhibition of template function
optionExplanations: Correct. Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that binds to DNA, interfering with its function and replication in Mycobacterium leprae.
M2 proton channel blockade is the mechanism of Amantadine, an anti-influenza agent.
Blockade of the 50S ribosomal subunit is characteristic of macrolides and chloramphenicol.
Ergosterol binding and membrane permeability alteration is the mechanism of polyene antifungals like Amphotericin B.
Competing with PABA for folic acid synthesis is the mechanism of Dapsone and other sulfonamides.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page)-407: Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA... causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Chemically, Dapsone is classified as which of the following?
options: Phenazine dye
8-aminoquinoline
4-aminoquinoline
Diaminodiphenylsulfone
Nitroimidazole
correctOption: Diaminodiphenylsulfone
optionExplanations: Phenazine dye is the class for Clofazimine.
8-aminoquinoline is the class for Primaquine.
4-aminoquinoline is the class for Chloroquine.
Correct. Dapsone is chemically identified as diaminodiphenylsulfone.
Nitroimidazole is the class for Metronidazole and Tinidazole.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 45-year-old male is diagnosed with lepromatous leprosy. To minimize the development of antimicrobial resistance, the standard World Health Organization (WHO) recommended protocol suggests utilizing a multidrug therapy (MDT). Which of the following drugs serves as the backbone of this combination, acting as a competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase in Mycobacterium leprae?
options: Ethionamide
Dapsone
Acedapsone
Clofazimine
Rifampin
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Ethionamide is a second-line antitubercular agent; although it has some activity against mycobacteria, it is not part of the standard primary WHO MDT for leprosy.
Dapsone is a sulfone that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of folic acid in M. leprae, similar to the action of sulfonamides.
Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone used for long-term inhibition but is not the standard immediate-acting backbone of the primary oral MDT protocol.
Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that interacts with DNA; while used in MDT, its mechanism does not involve dihydropteroate synthase inhibition.
Rifampin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It is a bactericidal component of leprosy MDT but does not interfere with the folic acid pathway.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae. The mechanism of action of sulfones may involve inhibition of folic acid synthesis. Because of increasing reports of resistance, it is recommended that the drug be used in combinations with rifampin and/or clofazimine.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A patient being treated for leprosy with a multidrug regimen presents with significant red-brown skin discoloration and complains of persistent abdominal cramping. Which pharmacological agent in the standard MDT protocol for leprosy is most likely responsible for these specific clinical findings?
options: Clofazimine
Rifampin
Ethionamide
Dapsone
Thalidomide
correctOption: Clofazimine
optionExplanations: Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that accumulates in tissues, leading to a classic red-brown to black skin discoloration and frequent gastrointestinal irritation.
Rifampin is known to cause orange discoloration of bodily fluids (urine, sweat, tears) rather than semi-permanent dark skin pigmentation.
Ethionamide is a second-line agent that primarily causes severe gastrointestinal irritation and neurologic effects, but not generalized skin hyperpigmentation.
Dapsone typically causes methemoglobinemia or hemolysis, not the characteristic red-brown/black pigmentary changes of the skin.
Thalidomide is used for erythema nodosum leprosum (an immunologic reaction to leprosy), but it does not cause the specified skin pigment changes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page)-407: Drug regimens usually include combinations of dapsone with rifampin... with or without clofazimine. Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA, causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: In the management of leprosy, clinicians often distinguish between the primary bactericidal effect and the suppression of drug resistance. Which drug in the WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (MDT) is utilized specifically to delay the emergence of resistance to sulfones and is characterized by its ability to inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase?
options: Clofazimine
Primaquine
Dapsone
Rifampin
Minocycline
correctOption: Rifampin
optionExplanations: Clofazimine is a phenazine dye that acts on DNA directly, but the text specifically highlights rifampin's role in delaying dapsone resistance.
Primaquine is an antimalarial tissue schizonticide and has no therapeutic role in the standard MDT for leprosy.
Dapsone is the primary drug against which resistance develops; therefore, it is the agent being protected, not the agent used to delay resistance to itself.
Rifampin is a potent bactericidal agent that inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. In leprosy protocols, it is crucial for preventing resistance to dapsone.
Minocycline is mentioned as a potential antibiotic for nontuberculous mycobacteria but is not a standard component of the first-line WHO leprosy MDT.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 38-year-old male with a history of recurrent skin lesions is diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy. One week after starting a multidrug therapy (MDT) containing dapsone, he presents to the clinic with profound fatigue, jaundice, and dark-colored urine. Laboratory tests confirm a significant drop in hemoglobin and a diagnosis of acute hemolytic anemia. Which underlying patient factor must be assessed to explain this pharmacological reaction to the standard leprosy protocol?
options: Renal creatinine clearance
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) levels
Plasma protein binding capacity
Thymidine kinase activity
Hepatic acetyltransferase genotype
correctOption: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) levels
optionExplanations: Renal clearance is important for dapsone elimination, but it does not mechanistically explain a rapid onset of acute hemolytic anemia.
Dapsone is a cellular oxidant. In patients with G6PD deficiency, the lack of NADPH leads to an inability to maintain glutathione, resulting in oxidative hemolysis.
While dapsone is widely distributed, competition for plasma protein binding is more characteristic of sulfonamides and their drug interactions, not acute hemolysis.
Thymidine kinase is involved in the activation of antiherpes drugs (like acyclovir), not the toxicological pathways of sulfones in leprosy.
Acetyltransferase genotype affects isoniazid (INH) metabolism in tuberculosis, but dapsone-induced acute hemolysis is primarily linked to G6PD status.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone)... Hemolysis may occur, especially in patients with G6PDH deficiency.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: To facilitate long-term compliance in the management of leprosy, a repository formulation of the primary sulfone is available that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months. What is the name of this pharmacological derivative used in specific leprosy management strategies?
options: Melarsoprol
Metrifonate
Acedapsone
Stibogluconate
Suramin
correctOption: Acedapsone
optionExplanations: Melarsoprol is an organic arsenical used for the CNS stage of African sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis).
Metrifonate is an organophosphate used as an alternative drug for Schistosoma haematobium, not for mycobacterial infections.
Acedapsone is the repository (long-acting) injectable form of dapsone, designed to provide therapeutic levels over several months for leprosy patients.
Sodium stibogluconate is a pentavalent antimonial used for all forms of leishmaniasis, not leprosy.
Suramin is used for the early stages of trypanosomiasis and onchocerciasis, not as a repository sulfone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: According to standard clinical pharmacokinetics of leprosy medications, which component of the multidrug therapy (MDT) is known to undergo significant enterohepatic cycling before being eliminated primarily in the urine as acetylated metabolites?
options: Ethionamide
Mupirocin
Clofazimine
Rifampin
Dapsone
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Ethionamide is a second-line drug with significant GI and neurologic side effects, but its primary description does not focus on enterohepatic cycling/acetylation in this context.
Mupirocin is used topically and is not absorbed systemically; it has no role in the oral MDT for leprosy.
Clofazimine is a phenazine dye with a different metabolic pathway involving tissue accumulation rather than significant urinary acetylated metabolites.
Rifampin undergoes enterohepatic cycling, but it is eliminated mainly in the feces (colored orange), whereas the question specifies urinary acetylated metabolites.
Dapsone is specifically described as undergoing enterohepatic cycling and being excreted in the urine as acetylated derivatives.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone... can be given orally, penetrates tissues well, undergoes enterohepatic cycling, and is eliminated in the urine, partly as acetylated metabolites.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: During the management of a patient with multibacillary leprosy, the clinician notes that the patient is also being treated for a co-existing condition with warfarin. Which component of the standard leprosy MDT is most likely to reduce the anticoagulant efficacy of warfarin, requiring an adjustment in the patient's cardiovascular drug regimen?
options: Dapsone
Clofazimine
Paromomycin
Tinidazole
Rifampin
correctOption: Rifampin
optionExplanations: Dapsone may interact with some drugs, but it is not a potent inducer of hepatic P450 enzymes like rifampin.
Clofazimine does not have well-documented potent enzyme-inducing properties that would significantly reduce the half-life of warfarin.
Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that is minimally absorbed and would not interact with hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes.
Tinidazole is an anti-amebic agent that can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol but does not typically induce warfarin metabolism.
Rifampin is a classic inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, which increases the metabolism and thus reduces the efficacy of warfarin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): Rifampin strongly induces liver drug-metabolizing enzymes and enhances the elimination rate of many drugs, including... warfarin.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 40-year-old female is diagnosed with paucibacillary leprosy. Following the standard WHO MDT protocol, she is prescribed dapsone and rifampin. She is currently also using a combination oral contraceptive pill (OCP). What is the most critical pharmacological counseling she should receive regarding the interaction between her leprosy treatment and her OCP?
options: The MDT regimen will inhibit the renal excretion of the OCP
The OCP will inhibit the bioactivation of dapsone
Dapsone will displace the OCP from plasma proteins, increasing toxicity
Rifampin will induce OCP metabolism, increasing the risk of unintended pregnancy
Dapsone and the OCP will synergistically increase the risk of hemolysis
correctOption: Rifampin will induce OCP metabolism, increasing the risk of unintended pregnancy
optionExplanations: The interaction is metabolic (hepatic), not based on the inhibition of renal excretion pathways.
Dapsone is already active and does not require complex bioactivation that would be inhibited by contraceptive steroids.
Displacement from plasma proteins is a mechanism associated with sulfonamides, but rifampin's induction is the clinically dominant interaction here.
Rifampin induces hepatic microsomal enzymes, which accelerates the breakdown of estrogen/progestin in oral contraceptives, potentially failing to prevent ovulation.
There is no significant synergism between standard OCPs and dapsone regarding the mechanism of hemolysis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 391 (Book Page): Rifampin strongly induces liver drug-metabolizing enzymes and enhances the elimination rate of many drugs, including... contraceptive steroids.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A patient with leprosy presents with sudden onset of headache and dizziness. Laboratory findings include elevated methemoglobin levels in the blood. Which component of the standard multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy is most frequently associated with the induction of methemoglobinemia as a toxic adverse effect?
options: Amikacin
Minocycline
Dapsone
Clofazimine
Rifabutin
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside associated with nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not methemoglobinemia.
Minocycline is a tetracycline that can cause tooth discoloration and vestibular toxicity, but not methemoglobinemia.
Dapsone is a sulfone that can oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin, leading to cyanosis and symptoms of reduced oxygen delivery.
Clofazimine's primary systemic toxicities are gastrointestinal and pigmentary; it does not typically cause methemoglobinemia.
Rifabutin is a rifamycin derivative that can color fluids orange but is not primarily associated with methemoglobinemia.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Common adverse effects [of dapsone] include gastrointestinal irritation, fever, skin rashes, and methemoglobinemia.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: In the WHO-recommended multidrug protocol for the treatment of leprosy, what is the chemical classification of Dapsone, the primary agent used to inhibit M. leprae?
options: Aminoglycoside
Phenazine dye
Diaminodiphenylsulfone
Rifamycin derivative
Nitroimidazole
correctOption: Diaminodiphenylsulfone
optionExplanations: Aminoglycosides include streptomycin or amikacin, which are sometimes used for other mycobacteria but not as the backbone of the oral leprosy MDT.
Clofazimine is the phenazine dye in the leprosy MDT regimen.
Dapsone is chemically classified as a diaminodiphenylsulfone.
Rifampin and rifabutin are rifamycin derivatives, not dapsone.
Nitroimidazoles include metronidazole and tinidazole, which are not used in the standard leprosy protocol.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: According to standard protocols for the management of leprosy, which agent is specifically recommended to be administered monthly in a combination regimen to delay the emergence of resistance to dapsone?
options: Ethambutol
Pyrazinamide
Acedapsone
Rifampin
Clofazimine
correctOption: Rifampin
optionExplanations: Ethambutol is a first-line drug for tuberculosis that inhibits arabinosyltransferases in the cell wall, but it is not a standard component of the primary WHO-recommended regimens for leprosy management.

Pyrazinamide is an anti-mycobacterial drug used primarily in short-course tuberculosis treatment and requires acidic environments for activation; it is not utilized in the standard therapeutic protocols for leprosy.
Acedapsone is a long-acting repository form of dapsone itself, rather than a secondary agent added to a regimen specifically to prevent resistance to dapsone.

Rifampin is a potent bactericidal agent that inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. In leprosy protocols, its monthly administration is a strategic pharmacological step intended to prevent the development of resistant strains of M. leprae to dapsone.

Clofazimine is a phenazine dye used in leprosy regimens, but it is typically administered as part of a daily or monthly combination to treat the disease itself, not specifically cited in the text as the monthly agent to delay dapsone resistance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): In leprosy, rifampin given monthly delays the emergence of resistance to dapsone.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: The mechanism of action of the most active drug used in the chemotherapy of Mycobacterium leprae primarily involves which of the following biochemical pathways?
options: Inhibition of folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of arabinosyltransferase enzymes
Interference with DNA polymerization via phenazine dyes
Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Disruption of mycolic acid cell wall synthesis
correctOption: Inhibition of folic acid synthesis
optionExplanations: Dapsone, the most active agent against M. leprae, belongs to the sulfone subclass. Its mechanism is similar to sulfonamides, involving the competitive inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase, thus blocking the synthesis of folic acid.
Inhibition of arabinosyltransferase is the mechanism of ethambutol, used in the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis but not Mycobacterium leprae.
Interference with DNA via phenazine dyes describes the proposed mechanism for clofazimine, which is used in multibacillary leprosy but is distinct from the primary sulfone action.
Inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is the mechanism of action for rifampin, which is used in leprosy but is not the drug described as the most active sulfone-based agent.
Inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis is the mechanism of isoniazid (INH), which is a primary drug for tuberculosis but is not used in the standard treatment of leprosy.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae. The mechanism of action of sulfones may involve inhibition of folic acid synthesis.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
coreConcept: Adverse effects of Clofazimine vs. Sulfones
statement: When managing a patient with leprosy, a physician must distinguish between the adverse effects of different components. Which of the following effects is uniquely associated with the phenazine dye used in multibacillary regimens compared to sulfones?
options: Peripheral neuropathy
Methemoglobinemia
Red-brown to black skin discoloration
Hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients
Systemic lupus erythematosus-like syndrome
correctOption: Red-brown to black skin discoloration
optionExplanations: Peripheral neuropathy is more commonly associated with drugs like isoniazid or vincristine, rather than the primary drugs used in leprosy.
Methemoglobinemia is a common toxicity associated with the use of dapsone in the treatment of leprosy.
Clofazimine is known to accumulate in tissues and cause a characteristic skin discoloration that ranges from red-brown to nearly black, which is a major aesthetic concern for patients.
Hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients is a classic adverse effect associated with dapsone and other sulfones, rather than clofazimine.
A lupus-like syndrome is a known rare side effect of isoniazid (INH), not the standard agents used in leprosy management.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Clofazimine, a phenazine dye that may interact with DNA, causes gastrointestinal irritation and skin discoloration ranging from red-brown to nearly black.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 34-year-old male presents with multiple anaesthetic, hypopigmented skin patches and palpable thickening of the ulnar nerves. A diagnosis of leprosy is confirmed. The patient has a known history of severe favism. Which of the following drugs, as a standard component of the most active leprosy treatment, requires the most caution in this patient?
options: Rifabutin
Rifampin
Acedapsone
Dapsone
Clofazimine
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Rifabutin is a rifamycin used as an alternative to rifampin, particularly in HIV patients, but it does not share the specific oxidant risk of dapsone.
Rifampin is not typically associated with acute hemolytic crises in patients with G6PD deficiency; its main toxicities include liver dysfunction and orange discoloration of fluids.
Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone. While it would also be dangerous, Dapsone is the primary active agent used in daily oral regimens that requires immediate monitoring for acute hemolysis.
Dapsone is an oxidant drug. In patients with G6PD deficiency (often presenting as favism), it can lead to severe oxidative stress in erythrocytes, resulting in hemolysis and hemolytic anemia.
Clofazimine is associated with skin discoloration and gastrointestinal distress but does not typically cause oxidative hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Hemolysis may occur, especially in patients with G6PDH deficiency. (Section: Dapsone).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
coreConcept: Rationale for combination therapy in Leprosy
statement: In the pharmacological management of leprosy, why is the standard therapeutic protocol almost always composed of drug combinations rather than monotherapy?
options: To ensure the drugs can cross the blood-brain barrier
To delay the emergence of resistance and enhance efficacy
To bypass the need for hepatic acetylation of isoniazid
To reduce the gastrointestinal irritation caused by clofazimine
To increase the oral bioavailability of dapsone
correctOption: To delay the emergence of resistance and enhance efficacy
optionExplanations: Standard leprosy drugs like dapsone already penetrate tissues well; combination therapy is not primarily used to enhance CNS penetration in this context.

Mycobacteria, including M. leprae, are prone to developing resistance if treated with a single agent. Using combinations like dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine ensures that different pathways are targeted, delaying resistance and increasing the likelihood of cure.
Isoniazid is not a standard drug for leprosy, and its acetylation is a genetic trait of the host, not a reason for drug combinations in leprosy.
While combination therapy is the standard, it often increases the overall side-effect profile rather than reducing the specific irritation caused by clofazimine.
Combination therapy does not significantly alter the oral bioavailability of dapsone, which is already well absorbed.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 397 (Book Page): Chemotherapy of mycobacterial infections almost always involves the use of drug combinations to delay the emergence of resistance and to enhance antimycobacterial efficacy.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: Which of the following compounds is chemically classified as a diaminodiphenylsulfone and remains the most active single agent against Mycobacterium leprae?
options: Suramin
Clofazimine
Rifampin
Thalidomide
Dapsone
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Suramin is an antiprotozoal drug used for trypanosomiasis, not leprosy.
Clofazimine is a phenazine dye, not a diaminodiphenylsulfone.
Rifampin is a rifamycin derivative and an inhibitor of RNA polymerase.
Thalidomide is used for certain complications of leprosy (like Erythema Nodosum Leprosum) but is not a primary antimicrobial sulfone.
Dapsone is chemically a sulfone (diaminodiphenylsulfone). It is the cornerstone of leprosy treatment due to its high activity against the organism.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone) remains the most active drug against M leprae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months is known as:
options: Rifapentine
Dextromethorphan
Acedapsone
Ethionamide
Clofazimine
correctOption: Acedapsone
optionExplanations: Rifapentine is a rifamycin with a long half-life used in tuberculosis, but it is not a derivative of dapsone.
Dextromethorphan is an antitussive drug and has no role in the management of leprosy.
Acedapsone is the repository (depot) formulation of dapsone. It is used to provide long-lasting inhibitory levels of the drug, which can be useful in improving compliance in certain settings.
Ethionamide is a second-line drug for tuberculosis and is not a repository sulfone.
Clofazimine is a dye used orally and does not serve as a repository form of sulfones.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 399 (Book Page): Acedapsone is a repository form of dapsone that provides inhibitory plasma concentrations for several months.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
statement: A 45-year-old patient being treated for leprosy presents with new-onset fatigue and dark urine. Physical examination reveals slight jaundice. Laboratory tests indicate an increased reticulocyte count and the presence of Heinz bodies in the peripheral smear. Which component of his antimicrobial therapy is most likely responsible for this metabolic complication?
options: Rifampin
Ethambutol
Dapsone
Clofazimine
Pyrazinamide
correctOption: Dapsone
optionExplanations: Rifampin can cause orange discoloration of urine, but it does not cause Heinz body formation or reticulocytosis associated with oxidative hemolysis.
Ethambutol is associated with optic neuritis but does not cause hematological oxidative stress.
Dapsone is a well-known oxidant. In susceptible individuals or at high doses, it causes oxidative damage to hemoglobin, leading to the formation of Heinz bodies and subsequent hemolysis.
Clofazimine causes skin discoloration but is not typically associated with hemolytic anemia or Heinz bodies.
Pyrazinamide is not used in leprosy and typically causes hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity.
